title: It is passing
hook: beet jaihai: it is passing, life is passing in vain (Jaijavanti M9, ang 1352)

segments.voice: Yesterday, remember: remembering the Lord is your real work. Today's hymn, in the same raga, asks what happens when that work is left undone.

Forty minutes. That's how long the phone held on before you looked up. Not spent, exactly. Just gone. You can't say what you saw. You weren't resting and you weren't working. The time slipped through without leaving a mark. Now stretch that out. A month like that. A year. Guru Tegh Bahadur's next hymn in Raag Jaijavanti opens with two words, said twice, like a clock ticking: beet jaihai, beet jaihai.
screen: `FORTY MINUTES, GONE.` → `A MONTH, A YEAR.` → `BEET JAIHAI, BEET JAIHAI.`

segments.voice: The full line is beet jaihai, beet jaihai, janam akaaj re. It is passing, it is passing: life, without its work. Beet is to pass, to slip by. And akaaj links back to yesterday. Kaaj was your work; akaaj is without the work, idle, done for nothing. Yesterday's hymn said remembering is your kaaj. Today's says what life becomes without it. Then, in paraphrase: night and day you hear the scriptures recited, and still you don't understand, unknowing one. Death has already arrived; where will you run? The body you thought was permanent will turn to dust. Why don't you take the Lord's Name? The word for what's heard is puraan, the old sacred stories people listened to recited. But the fault isn't in the stories. It's hearing holy words without letting them in, and that can happen to anyone, including someone who hears Gurbani every morning and lets it slide past like background music. Then the hymn turns. In paraphrase: bring devotion to the Lord into your heart, and let go of the mind's pride. Says Nanak, this is the way to live in the world, shining. The word is biraaj, to dwell in splendor, like a king on a throne. So the hymn starts with a ticking clock and ends with a person living brightly. The passing is real; what fills it is up to us. Said slowly, the line isn't grim. It's a wake-up call: it is passing, so live it.
screen: `BEET JAIHAI: IT IS PASSING.` · `AKAAJ: LIFE WITHOUT ITS WORK.` · `HEARING WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING.` · `BIRAAJ: LIVE IN SPLENDOR.` · then, large: `IT IS PASSING.`

segments.voice: Look at the next few hours of your day and choose one, then decide what would make that hour not akaaj, not empty: work done with full attention, a walk with someone you love, real rest, or time with a shabad. Then let the plan go and simply breathe, feeling this minute pass, fully. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Beet, passing, slipping by. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn warns, beet jaihai, that life passes akaaj, without its work, and ends with the way to live shining in the world.
Your line: live in the world, shining. Biraaj: a life lit up, not just used up. That's today.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti shabad 'beet jaihai beet jaihai' is sung in kirtan; Sikhs often hear its ticking refrain as a call to fill life with remembrance and devotion.

fork.setup: the hymn has warned that life is passing without its work. what does it say to do?
options: panic and work harder at everything.
bring devotion into the heart and let go of pride.
give up, since time is running out anyway.
fork.reveal: bring devotion to the Lord into your heart and drop the mind's pride; says Nanak, this is how to live shining in the world.

original.note: Gurmukhi: beet, passing, slipping by. The hymn says it twice, like a clock: beet jaihai, beet jaihai.

trapdoor: what you thought: it is passing is a gloomy thing to say.
what it means: it's a wake-up call; life passes, so fill it with its real work.
what a scholar hears: the hymn plays kaaj against akaaj, the work and its absence, linking it to the shabad before it in Raag Jaijavanti.

chat.says: Isn't 'life is passing' kind of a depressing thing to sing about?
options: It starts with a ticking clock but ends with living in the world, shining.
Yes, it's meant to scare people into hiding from the world until death comes.
It says nothing you do matters, so there's no point trying to fill the time.
chat.meaning: Beet jaihai warns that life can pass akaaj, without its work, then ends with biraaj: devotion, without pride, is the way to live shining.

akaaj.meaning: without its work, idle, done for nothing

puraan.meaning: the old sacred stories, heard recited

biraaj.meaning: to dwell in splendor, like a king on a throne
